title: Fetch is not pull
concept: git fetch, origin/main, then merge; fetch vs pull

story.speaker: Sam
story.text: I pushed the schedule page this morning. Did you get it?

story.speaker: Ada
story.text: Not yet. Your laptop does not check the website on its own.

story.speaker: Ada
story.text: `git fetch` downloads new commits but does **not** change your files.

story.speaker: Ada
story.text: It updates a pointer called `origin/main`. That means "where main was online when I last looked".

story.speaker: Ada
story.text: Fetch first, look with `git log`, then `git merge origin/main` to actually get the files.

story.speaker: Ada
story.text: `git pull` is just those two steps in one. Doing them apart once shows you what pull hides.

items.text: Fetch to see what is new online
Bring Sam's work into your files

hints: Two steps: first download, then join the downloaded work into your branch.
`git fetch` downloads. `git merge origin/main` moves your branch up to match.
Run `git fetch`, answer the question, then run `git merge origin/main`.

questions.prompt: You ran git fetch. Is schedule.html in your folder yet?

choices.text: Yes, fetch copies files into my folder
No, fetch only downloaded the commits and moved origin/main

questions.explanation: Fetch never touches your files. It downloads commits and updates origin/main. A merge is what changes your folder.

recap: `git fetch` downloads commits and moves `origin/main`, but leaves your files alone. `git merge origin/main` brings them in. `git pull` does both at once.

cheatSheet.summary: Download new commits without changing your files
Join the downloaded commits into your branch
